summary:
Kaduna State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment and reaches well beyond marriage: it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years. Human Rights Watch (October 2016), in 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', records police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under the Act.

Kaduna adds two further layers of its own on top of the federal statute. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) documents this two-layer criminalisation: Kaduna's secular Penal Code, adopted in 2017, punishes 'unnatural offences' including sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality under Section 259 with up to 21 years' imprisonment plus a fine, a ceiling above the federal 14-year maximum; alongside it, Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 applies to Muslims as a parallel criminal code.

Kaduna is one of twelve northern states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, a bloc created when Zamfara's governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation. Kaduna's own instrument is Law No. 4 of 2002, signed and brought into operation on 21 June 2002 (Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36, 4 July 2002, pp. A15-A108, bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code). Its enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), with no unmarried or married graduation, and the corresponding offence between women is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment at the discretion of the qadi. Kaduna is one of only three states whose enacted text carries that explicit capital sentence. The Home Office note's section 8.4.3 reproduces this Kaduna row: death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy).

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. The Home Office note records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Sahara Reporters (August 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria, relays warnings of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Trans visitors face lethal violence followed by official misgendering and impunity. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. Six months later, in February 2025, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Police use the national law against people for how they appear. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'. Those affected describe the Act as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Enforcement takes the form of mass arrests at social venues across the country: men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011; more than 100 party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.
tangentialFactors:
Kaduna's own secular ceiling sits above the federal one. Section 259 of the Kaduna Penal Code of 2017 provides up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine for sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality, where the federal Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 stops at 14 years. The Home Office note carries both figures side by side, so a visitor facing charges in Kaduna is exposed to a longer term than the national headline figure.

The Sharia layer in Kaduna is unusually severe even within the twelve-state bloc. Of the northern states that adopted Sharia into their criminal legislation between 1999 and 2002, only three, Kaduna among them, enacted text stating an unqualified stoning-to-death sentence for sodomy with no graduation by marital status; elsewhere the capital penalty is graded or qualified. Kaduna's Law No. 4 of 2002 has been in operation since 21 June 2002 and is bound with a Sharia Criminal Procedure Code, so it is a promulgated parallel code rather than a set of interpretive rulings.

A decade-outcome assessment of the national statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the Act, finds the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Cross-dressing has been proposed as a discrete offence. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing, a measure that would target presentation directly rather than conduct.

Imprisonment of a prominent transgender woman raised placement questions. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kaduna State are subject to two criminal codes at once. Muslims fall under the Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 alongside the state's secular Penal Code, and the Home Office note records the two-layer regime as in force: a harsher Kaduna-specific secular statute plus a parallel Sharia layer. Section 259 of the 2017 Penal Code covers 'unnatural offences' defined as sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality.

Same-sex conduct between women in Kaduna is left to judicial discretion rather than a fixed tariff. The 2002 law's annotation places the offence under ta'azir, punishable at the discretion of the qadi, while the male offence carries the fixed capital sentence.

Community health and advocacy work carries arrest risk. Activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work, and many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes.

Openly LGBTQ-friendly congregations and organisations have been exposed by press publication. The House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008, after which some members were threatened, beaten and stoned. The national Act's ban on the operation of gay organisations constrains organised community life.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kaduna-specific enforcement record is sourced. The inventory contains no arrests, prosecutions or sentences under Section 259 of the Kaduna Penal Code 2017 or under Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law 2002, and no Kaduna-specific incident data for the period covered. The mass-arrest figures cited (Bauchi 2007, Asaba and Egbeda 2018, Warri 2023, Gombe 2023) all come from other states and illustrate the national pattern.

Whether Kaduna's Sharia layer reaches non-Muslim residents or visitors is not stated in the sources. The Home Office note describes the Sharia layer as applying to Muslims, and the inventory does not resolve how the two Kaduna codes allocate jurisdiction across religious identity.

The status of the proposed cross-dressing offence is unresolved. Reuters (September 2022) records fear of the proposal among transgender Nigerians, but no source in the inventory confirms whether legislation was introduced, passed or abandoned.

Trans-specific documentation rules are not sourced. No source addresses legal gender recognition in Kaduna or Nigeria, marker or passport treatment of trans travellers, airport or border screening that risks outing, or facilities access rules. The federal statute's application to gender expression rests on the cross-dressing proposal and press treatment of placement, not on an enacted gender-identity provision.
